cues.text: A New Extreme: Eutychianism
The condemnation of Nestorius at Ephesus in 431 did not end Christological controversy — it provoked an opposite error.
An elderly Constantinopolitan archimandrite named Eutyches was eager to guard against anything resembling Nestorius's division of Christ into two persons.
He began teaching that after the Incarnation, Christ's humanity was effectively absorbed into his divinity, leaving only one nature — a position later called Monophysitism ("one-nature-ism").

Where Nestorius had erred, in the Church's judgment, by pulling Christ's two natures too far apart, Eutyches erred in the opposite direction, blending them so completely that Christ's humanity was no longer, in any meaningful sense, like ours.
Both extremes threatened the same underlying conviction that had driven the councils since Nicaea: that in Christ, God had truly and fully entered human experience without ceasing to be God.

Eutyches was condemned by a local synod at Constantinople in 448, but he had powerful backers, including the imperial chamberlain and Patriarch Dioscorus of Alexandria , who saw an opportunity to extend Alexandria's theological influence at Antioch's and Constantinople's expense.
A council convened at Ephesus in 449 and was later branded the "Robber Council" ( Latrocinium ) by Pope St. Leo for its bullying tactics.
Soldiers reportedly intimidated bishops into signing blank documents.
The council exonerated Eutyches and deposed his chief opponents by force, leaving the Christological question in worse disorder than before.
Pope Leo's Tome
Pope St. Leo the Great had already sent a carefully argued doctrinal letter, the Tome of Leo , to Constantinople ahead of the 449 council.
It set out a clear formula: Christ is one Person existing in two complete and unconfused natures, divine and human, each retaining its own properties while united without division or separation.
The Robber Council had refused even to have Leo's letter read aloud.
With the death of Emperor Theodosius II in 450, his sister Pulcheria and her husband, the new emperor Marcian , were both firmly orthodox.
They moved quickly to reverse the disorder of 449, summoning a new, larger council to meet at Chalcedon , across the Bosphorus from Constantinople, in October 451.
The Council and Its Definition
Some 350 to 600 bishops attended Chalcedon, making it by far the largest of the early councils and overwhelmingly Eastern in composition, with the West represented chiefly by legates of Pope Leo.
Sessions were held in the church of St. Euphemia, and the debates were recorded in unusually full detail, giving historians one of the richest surviving records of any ancient council in action.
When Leo's Tome was finally read to the assembly, the bishops are recorded as acclaiming, "Peter has spoken through Leo."
Dioscorus of Alexandria was deposed for his conduct at the Robber Council, not for heresy as such.
Eutyches's teaching was formally condemned.

The council's Chalcedonian Definition declared that Christ is "acknowledged in two natures, without confusion, without change, without division, without separation" — one Person, fully God and fully man, the properties of each nature preserved and united in a single subsistence.
The formula was crafted to exclude both Nestorius's error of dividing Christ into two persons and Eutyches's error of blending his two natures into one.
A Painful Division
Not every church accepted Chalcedon's formula.

Sizeable communities in Egypt, Syria, Armenia, and Ethiopia held that the council's language, however carefully worded, still leaned too far toward Nestorius, and they broke communion with Constantinople and Rome rather than accept it.
These communities survive today as the Oriental Orthodox churches.
The schism Chalcedon left in its wake — the most lasting rupture among the early councils — has never been fully healed, though modern ecumenical dialogue has clarified much common ground.

The council also passed twenty-eight disciplinary canons, including the contested Canon 28 granting Constantinople patriarchal privileges "equal to" those of Rome, which Pope Leo's legates refused to accept as compatible with Rome's unique Petrine primacy.
Legacy
Chalcedon's definition of Christ as one Person in two natures became, and remains, the touchstone of Catholic Christology.
It was cited at every subsequent council that addressed the nature of Christ.
It stands alongside Nicaea's homoousios as one of the two great conciliar formulas underlying all later Catholic teaching on the Trinity and the Incarnation.
Its formula did not end controversy—the Monophysite schism it produced persists to this day among the Oriental Orthodox churches.
But it gave the Church a precise, durable vocabulary for confessing a mystery.
Nicaea, Constantinople, and Ephesus had each addressed it from a different angle: in Jesus Christ, true God and true man are united, undivided and unconfused, in a single Person.
The two emperors who convened the council, Marcian and his empress Pulcheria, are venerated as saints in the Eastern Church.
Their role in restoring order to Christological debate reminds us how closely doctrine and empire remained intertwined throughout this era of the councils.
